title: How To Get Your Class Back On Track Fast
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recounts a personal experience of returning to a new high school class after missing over a week to the flu, only to find their behavior had unraveled under a substitute who never held them accountable. Rather than panic, he treated the situation as an opportunity to test how quickly his classroom management principles could restore order. After confirming the depth of the disengagement through a deliberately disastrous group assignment, he stopped the class, taught an explicit lesson on entering the room and behaving during attendance, and reminded them of consequences before starting fresh — with immediate, visible improvement. He credits two advantages: having thoroughly taught expectations before getting sick, and unwavering confidence in the approach itself. He connects the lesson to basketball coach John Wooden's famous attention to small details, like teaching players to put on their socks properly, arguing that mastering fundamentals transfers to everything else. The piece closes by emphasizing that this reteaching strategy works at any grade level and produces not just compliance but genuine calm and motivation.
points: A substitute's lack of accountability can unravel a class's culture within just days, even after strong expectations were set.
Deliberately letting a lapse play out briefly can reveal exactly how far behavior has slipped before intervening.
Stopping the class to explicitly reteach a routine — like entering the room and behaving during attendance — resets expectations fast.
Small, seemingly minor details, echoing John Wooden's famous sock-teaching lesson, transfer into excellence across all behavior.
The reteaching strategy works the same way regardless of grade level, from first graders to high schoolers.
quotes: When I returned, it was as if my new class had never met me.
There had been little direction and absolutely no accountability. Now it appeared that the students were in charge.
In the days before coming down with the flu, I laid out exactly what was expected of them, academically and behaviorally.
At the beginning of every season, he would teach his players how to put on their socks. The idea was that if they could do this one thing well, they could do all things well.
I sent them back to their seats (to groans). And I taught them a lesson on how we, the class, enter the room and listen during attendance.

The most gratifying thing about the experience, however, and the most striking change, was their happiness and sense of calm well-being in knowing exactly where they stood and what they needed to do to succeed.
It’s clear and comforting. It’s highly and intrinsically motivational. It’s how education should be.
